Consult Summary:
- Patient with known heart failure presents with progressive dyspnea on exertion, dry cough, and bilateral ankle edema over two weeks, worsen-ing in the last few days; assessment favors possible heart failure exacerbation with plan to optimize diuresis and obtain cardiac investigations.

History:
- Presenting complaint:
  - Shortness of breath progressing over the last couple of weeks; markedly worse in the last few days.
  - Breathlessness with minimal exertion; previously able to walk to shops, now needs to sit to catch breath.
  - Dry cough.
  - Ankle swelling (bilateral).
  - No chest pain; no fever; no palpitations reported.
  - General health described as run-down but otherwise normal; appetite and hydration OK.
- Timeline:
  - Symptoms insidiously started over ~2 weeks; deterioration most prominent in the last few days.
- Exacerbating/relieving factors:
  - Exertion worsens symptoms; no noted relief strategies discussed.
- Associated symptoms/ROS:
  - Dry cough; bilateral ankle edema; no chest pain, fever, or significant weight changes noted.
- Past Medical History:
  - Known heart failure.
  - Prior event described as a “small heart attack” about 5 years ago; hospitalization for a few days; no ongoing details provided.
- Medications (current):
  - Furosemide (dose/route/frequency not documented).
  - Aspirin (dose not documented).
  - Bisoprolol (dose not documented).
- Allergies:
  - None stated.
- Social History:
  - Lives alone with two cats (Polly and Tim).
  - Works part-time as a lorry driver; daytime shifts; finds work exhausting when active.
  - Former smoker: about 1 pack/day for ~25 years; quit (date not specified).
  - Alcohol: does not drink.
  - Exercise: walks to shops daily; no regular running.
- Family History:
  - Father died of a heart attack in early 60s.
  - Mother with osteoporosis.
- Review of Systems:
  - Cardiorespiratory: dyspnea on exertion; dry cough; bilateral ankle edema; no chest pain or fevers reported.
  - Genitourinary: reports polyuria since starting diuretics (implied).
  - Others: appetite and intake described as OK.
- Summary impression from conversation:
  - Worsening heart failure symptoms suggesting possible decompensation.

Past Medical History:
- Heart failure (diagnosed prior to this visit).
- Prior myocardial event described as a “small heart attack” ~5 years ago; brief hospitalization; no ongoing details provided.
- Medications:
  - Furosemide (dose/route/frequency not documented).
  - Aspirin (dose not documented).
  - Bisoprolol (dose not documented).
- Allergies: None reported.

Social History:
- Lives alone with two cats.
- Occupation: part-time lorry driver; daytime shifts; reports work can be exhausting.
- Smoking: former smoker; ~1 pack/day for ~25 years; quit (date not specified).
- Alcohol: none.
- Exercise: daily walking to shops; not engaged in heavy exercise.

Family History:
- Father died of myocardial infarction in early 60s.
- Mother with osteoporosis; still living.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: Not documented in transcript.
- Exam findings noted by clinician:
  - Bilateral ankle edema described by patient and corroborated by clinician (edema present).
  - Clinician noted patient’s chest exam, oxygen saturations, and blood pressure were “OK” (numbers not provided).

Investigations:
- Planned:
  - Blood tests: full blood count; kidney function.
  - Echocardiogram (general scan of the heart) to assess pumping function.
- Prior imaging/records:
  - Patient recalls a prior echocardiogram; plan acknowledges repeating or reviewing as needed (not explicitly documented beyond plan).

Assessment & Plan:
- Issue 1: Possible heart failure decompensation/exacerbation
  - Plan:
    - Increase furosemide to two tablets daily for the first few days (exact dose not documented).
    - Schedule basic blood tests: full blood count and kidney function.
    - Arrange echocardiogram to assess cardiac function.
    - Follow-up in about one week to assess response; call sooner if symptoms worsen (increased breathlessness, chest pain, palpitations, dizziness).
    - Advise patient to seek prompt contact if symptoms deteriorate.
- General management considerations:
  - Address symptomatic relief for dyspnea and edema with diuretic adjustment.
  - Echocardiography for baseline/update of ventricular function.
  - Routine labs to evaluate anemia, renal function, and other contributors to dyspnea.

Quality checks:
- Missing but clinically expected elements:
  - Exact vital signs (blood pressure, heart rate, oxygen saturation, temperature) and weight are not documented.
  - Complete current medications with doses, routes, and frequencies documented (only drug names provided; dosages not specified).
  - Documentation of allergy status is present (no allergies reported), but formal med reconciliation details are incomplete.
- Internal conflicts:
  - None identified in the transcript; there is a minor patient-doctor naming confusion around bisoprolol/metoprolol, but it does not constitute a diagnostic conflict.
- Transcript quality:
  - Conversation contains routine clinical dialogue with minor audio/messaging gaps (e.g., intermittent connectivity); no critical clinical data appears contradictory or missing beyond noted items.
